references.text: The same threat of diseases as punishment for disobedience, including consumption (שַׁחֶפֶת) and fever (קַדַּחַת), is mentioned in the curses in Deuteronomy.
The theme that enemies will eat the fruit of your labor, so that you sow in vain, is repeated in the curses.
Describes how one sows much but harvests little, and others enjoy the fruit of one's labor.
Isaiah describes the opposite—the blessing where one enjoys the fruit of their own work—in contrast to the curse in Leviticus.
Hosea refers to disease and destruction as God's judgment on the people for their disobedience.
Amos describes how God struck the people with drought and blight, but they did not return to Him.
Haggai describes how the people sowed much but harvested little, paralleling the curse of sowing in vain.
Micah prophesies that one will sow but not reap, as a judgment on the people's sin.
Jeremiah warns that enemies will eat the harvest and bread, and devour all that the people have worked for.
